analysis.one_liner: Bans employers from recognizing a union unless workers choose one in a government-run secret ballot election.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or vote: it sat in the House Education and Labor Committee, then a subcommittee, until the Congress ended, despite 115 Republican cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would rewrite federal labor law to make it illegal for an employer to voluntarily recognize or bargain with a union unless a majority of workers first voted for that union in a secret ballot election run by the National Labor Relations Board. It would also make it illegal for a union to ask an employer for such recognition. Today, employers and unions can lawfully agree to recognize a union when a majority of workers sign authorization cards, sometimes through agreements where the employer stays neutral. The bill would shut down that route, leaving the government-run election as the only way a new union can be recognized.
analysis.who_benefits: Employers who do not want a union would benefit most. If the bill passed, unions could no longer sign card-check or neutrality agreements with employers, and workers could organize only through an NLRB election process that typically takes months, giving employers a long window to campaign against the union. Supporters say the bill protects workers from pressure during card-signing drives.

how_it_helps.text: The bill makes it an unfair labor practice for an employer to recognize or bargain with a union that was not chosen by a majority of employees in a secret ballot election conducted by the NLRB [S2, S3].

The bill's findings argue that a secret ballot is the only method that ensures a choice free of coercion, intimidation, irregularity, or illegality, and that recognition by private agreement threatens employees' freedom of choice [S3].
It makes it an unfair labor practice for a union to cause or attempt to cause an employer to grant recognition without such an election, closing off card-check and neutrality agreements [S2, S3].
It directs the NLRB to revise its regulations within six months of enactment to implement the secret ballot requirement [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Workers who want to join a union and unions themselves would bear the cost. Voluntary recognition through signed authorization cards is lawful today; the bill would make it illegal, leaving only the NLRB election route, which takes longer and gives employers time to campaign against organizing. Workers who prefer card-signing over an employer-contested election would lose that option.
analysis.who_pays_short: Workers seeking to organize and unions

drawbacks.text: The bill outlaws a method of union recognition that is lawful under current law. Voluntary recognition agreements, including card-check and neutrality agreements, would become an unfair labor practice on both the employer and union side, removing a path workers have used to unionize without a contested election [S2, S3].

The bill's one route — an NLRB secret ballot election — is typically a slow process, and the delay gives employers an extended period to campaign against the union before workers vote. Critics of election-only recognition argue this is why employers prefer elections over card checks.

Supporters would counter that card signing is conducted by union organizers in the open, with no privacy, and that the bill's secret ballot requirement protects employees from pressure from either side [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offers workers a private, government-supervised vote on union representation, which is a real protection. But it does so by banning a currently lawful alternative — voluntary recognition after majority card sign-up — and by removing any employer's ability to agree to stay neutral. The practical effect is that every organizing drive would run through a process that takes months and gives employers the longest opportunity to oppose it. Workers who wanted union representation would be the ones paying that price, while employers gain a single, slower route that they are better positioned to contest.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the House Education and Labor Committee in February 2009, moved to a subcommittee two months later, and never got a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the Congress ended in January 2011.

narrative.text: Rep. John Kline (R-MN) introduced the Secret Ballot Protection Act on February 25, 2009 [S1, S5].
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Education and Labor on the day it was introduced [S5].
On April 22, 2009, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health, Employment, Labor, and Pensions — its last action of the Congress [S5].
It accumulated 115 cosponsors, all Republicans, and no version ever received a vote in either chamber [S4, S5].
Democrats held 253 of 435 House seats and chaired the Education and Labor Committee, so the bill never advanced [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Unions and workers who want to organize are better off, because the card-check and voluntary recognition routes the bill would have banned remain lawful. Employers gained nothing, but they also faced no threat, since the Democratic majority never considered the bill — it was largely a message bill aimed at the rival Employee Free Choice Act.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Unions and workers seeking to organize

for.what_they_did: Introduced the Secret Ballot Protection Act on February 25, 2009.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 115 cosponsors were Republicans in the 178-member House Republican conference, with no Democratic cosponsors; the bill was referred in a House where Democrats held 253 of 435 seats [S1, S4].

industries.note: If passed, employers could never be asked to recognize a union through card-check or neutrality agreements, and every organizing drive would run through a months-long election process they can contest. Employer groups backed this approach as a counter to the Employee Free Choice Act. The bill died, so their position is unchanged from current law.

The bill would ban the voluntary recognition agreements unions rely on to organize quickly, including card-check deals, and would make asking an employer for recognition an unfair labor practice. Union organizing options would shrink to NLRB elections only.
